meta.title: Epithelium
meta.summary: A group of closely associated cells that perform similar functions and are related in structure.

blocks.name: Tissue
blocks.def: A group of closely associated cells that perform similar functions and are related in structure.

blocks.name: <term d="The sheet of tightly packed cells that covers surfaces and lines cavities and tubes.">Epithelium</term>
blocks.def: The tissue type responsible for covering (and lining) — see below.

blocks.name: <term d="The tissue that supports, binds and separates other tissues, rich in matrix between its cells.">Connective tissue</term>
blocks.def: The tissue type responsible for support.

blocks.name: Muscle tissue
blocks.def: The tissue type responsible for movement.

blocks.name: Nervous tissue
blocks.def: The tissue type responsible for control.

blocks.name: Epithelium (definition)
blocks.def: A sheet of cells tightly joined to one another that covers body surfaces, lines body cavities, and also forms the secretory portions of many glands.

blocks.x: Epithelial cells are closely packed together, always have a free surface (facing outward or into a lumen/cavity), and sit on a basement membrane that anchors them to the underlying connective tissue.

blocks.name: Covering/lining epithelium
blocks.def: Epithelium found on external and internal body surfaces.

blocks.name: Glandular (secretory) epithelium
blocks.def: The tissue that forms glands.

blocks.name: Functions of epithelium
blocks.def: Protection, absorption, sensory reception, ion transport, secretion, filtration, digestion, and lubrication — epithelium takes on many different arrangements to serve these varied roles.

blocks.name: Cellularity
blocks.def: Epithelium consists of many closely packed cells, with minimal extracellular material between them.

blocks.name: Regenerative capacity
blocks.def: Epithelium has a high capacity for self-renewal/repair.

blocks.name: Tight lateral adhesion
blocks.def: Epithelial cells have tight lateral adhesions; the lateral junctions between cells often form a sealing/adhesive structure called a junctional complex.

blocks.name: Avascular but innervated
blocks.def: Epithelium has no blood vessels of its own; it's nourished by diffusion from blood vessels in the underlying connective tissue, but does have nerve supply.

blocks.name: Polarity
blocks.def: The <term d="The free surface of a cell, facing the lumen or the outside world.">apical</term> (upper) surface of an epithelial cell faces a free surface or lumen and may bear <term d="Short hair-like projections that beat in waves to sweep fluid or particles along a surface.">cilia</term>/<term d="Tiny finger-like projections on a cell surface that greatly increase the area for absorption.">microvilli</term>; the basal (lower) surface contributes the basal lamina to the basement membrane.

blocks.x: The lateral surfaces of epithelial cells contain specialized junctions that let cells adhere to each other and restrict movement of materials between adjacent cells (the paracellular route).

blocks.cap: The major types of cell junction found in epithelial tissue.

blocks.name: Tight junctions
blocks.def: Junctions so close they can be nearly impermeable, sealing cells together to prevent lateral transfer of fluid and molecules. Made of two proteins, claudin and occludin. Found in the bladder, kidney, and intestine.

blocks.name: Desmosomes
blocks.def: Anchoring junctions that hold two cells together without being completely sealed — they allow water and ions (Na⁺, K⁺) to flow between cells. Filaments anchor to the opposite cell side. Found in skin, intestine, etc.

blocks.name: Adherens junctions
blocks.def: Transmembrane linker junctions made of actin filaments and cadherin (a calcium-dependent protein), forming a "belt" around the cell. Help epithelial surfaces resist separation during contractile activity. Found in intestinal epithelial cells.

blocks.name: Gap junctions
blocks.def: Channel-like junctions that let cells communicate rapidly via electrical signals, electrically coupling neighbouring cells. Critical for coordinating tissues like cardiac muscle (synchronized heartbeat) and the smooth muscle of the uterine wall during childbirth.

blocks.name: Hemidesmosomes
blocks.def: Small, stud-like structures at the basement membrane — not technically a cell-to-cell junction, since they link basal cells to the lamina lucida (part of the basement membrane) rather than to another cell.

blocks.x: Epithelia are classified along three independent axes: thickness, cell shape, and surface specialization.

blocks.name: Simple epithelium
blocks.def: A single layer of cells.

blocks.name: Stratified epithelium
blocks.def: More than one layer of cells; note that stratified epithelia are named according to the shape of the cells at the apical (surface) layer, not the deeper layers.

blocks.name: <term d="Flat, scale-like in shape — used to describe thin, plate-shaped cells.">Squamous</term> cells
blocks.def: Wider than tall (flat).

blocks.name: <term d="Roughly cube-shaped, about as tall as it is wide.">Cuboidal</term> cells
blocks.def: As tall as wide (cube-shaped).

blocks.name: <term d="Tall and column-shaped, noticeably taller than it is wide.">Columnar</term> cells
blocks.def: Taller than wide.

blocks.name: Cilia
blocks.def: Motile apical projections (~0.2 μm diameter, ~8 μm long) that transport extracellular materials like mucus, debris, or cells. Built from microtubules (a "9+2" ultrastructure); taper distally and arise from basal granules.

blocks.name: Microvilli
blocks.def: Non-motile, finger-like apical projections (~0.1 μm diameter, 0.5–1.0 μm long) that amplify surface area. Built from microfilaments (lack the "9+2" structure); surrounded by a glycocalyx layer; do not arise from basal granules.

blocks.name: <term d="Showing a banded, striped appearance under the microscope.">Striated</term>/brush border
blocks.def: Densely packed microvilli, seen in the small intestine and kidney respectively.

blocks.name: Stereocilia
blocks.def: Exceedingly long microvilli (8–10 μm) found in the male reproductive tract and the inner ear's membranous labyrinth.

blocks.name: Keratin
blocks.def: A tough protective protein making the epithelial surface less prone to scratching or tearing.

blocks.name: Goblet cells
blocks.def: Unicellular exocrine glands scattered within epithelium that secrete mucin, which combines with water to form mucus.

blocks.name: Simple squamous epithelium
blocks.def: A single layer of flat cells. Function: passive diffusion and filtration; secretes lubricating substances in serosae. Location: renal corpuscles, alveoli of the lungs, lining of the heart/blood/lymphatic vessels, and the ventral body cavity linings (serosae).

blocks.name: Endothelium
blocks.def: The specific name for simple squamous epithelium lining blood and lymphatic vessels (and the heart's interior).

blocks.name: Mesothelium
blocks.def: Simple squamous epithelium lining the closed body cavities (peritoneal, pleural, pericardial) and covering the organs (viscera) within them.

blocks.name: Simple cuboidal epithelium
blocks.def: A single layer of cube-shaped cells. Function: secretion and absorption. Location: kidney tubules (may bear microvilli here), ovary surface, and the secretory/duct portions of some glands (e.g. thyroid, pancreas).

blocks.name: Simple columnar epithelium
blocks.def: A single layer of tall cells, which may be ciliated or non-ciliated. Ciliated form lines the small bronchi and uterine tubes. Non-ciliated form lines the digestive tract (stomach to anal canal), gallbladder, and endocervix, and may contain mucus-secreting goblet cells.

blocks.name: Pseudostratified columnar epithelium
blocks.def: A simple epithelium that only looks stratified: all cells touch the basement membrane, but only the tallest cells reach the apical surface, and nuclei sit at varying heights. May contain goblet cells and bear cilia or stereocilia. The ciliated type lines the trachea and much of the upper respiratory tract; the non-ciliated type (with stereocilia) lines the vas deferens, epididymis, and ducts of large glands.

blocks.name: Stratified squamous epithelium
blocks.def: A thick membrane of several cell layers; basal cells are columnar/cuboidal and metabolically active, while surface cells are flattened. The thickest epithelial tissue, adapted for protection against abrasion, water loss, UV radiation, and microbes.

blocks.cap: Stratified squamous epithelium, showing the multilayered structure with flattened cells at the free surface.

blocks.name: Keratinized stratified squamous epithelium
blocks.def: Found on dry surfaces subject to wear (epidermis, gingiva, hard palate, tongue papillae). Surface cells are dead, lacking nuclei and cytoplasm, and contain the waterproof protein keratin.

blocks.name: Non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium
blocks.def: Found on wet surfaces subject to wear but protected from drying (esophagus, mouth, anus, vagina, endocervix, urethra).

blocks.name: Stratified cuboidal epithelium
blocks.def: Generally two layers of cube-shaped cells. Function: protection. Location: small and large ducts of mammary glands, salivary glands, and the largest sweat glands.

blocks.name: Stratified columnar epithelium
blocks.def: A rare tissue type, about 3–4 layers thick. Function: protection and secretion. Location: part of the male urethra, large ducts of some glands, and part of the conjunctiva of the eye.

blocks.name: Transitional epithelium (urothelium)
blocks.def: A specialized stratified epithelium whose cells change shape and stretch — basal cells are cuboidal/columnar, <term d="Closer to the surface of the body.">superficial</term> cells are dome-shaped or squamous ("umbrella cells") and often binucleated. Function: allows urinary organs to stretch while maintaining a protective, impermeable lining. Found only in the urinary system: calyces, ureters, bladder, and <term d="Nearer to the trunk or to the point where a limb attaches.">proximal</term> urethra.

blocks.cap: Transitional epithelium (urothelium), which changes shape between the relaxed and stretched (distended) states.

blocks.name: Epithelial metaplasia
blocks.def: The reversible conversion of one mature epithelial cell type to another, as an adaptive response to chronic stress, inflammation, or abnormal stimuli — arising from reprogrammed gene expression in epithelial stem cells. Example: Barrett's esophagus, where chronic acid reflux converts the esophagus's stratified squamous epithelium into a simple columnar epithelium with goblet cells.

blocks.name: Gland
blocks.def: A cell or group of cells that synthesizes substances for release — either into the bloodstream (endocrine, ductless) or into a body cavity/outer surface (exocrine, via a duct). Epithelium forms glands by invaginating into the underlying connective tissue.

blocks.cap: The formation and structure of exocrine glands from invaginating epithelium.

blocks.name: Exocrine vs. endocrine glands
blocks.def: Exocrine glands have ducts and release their product onto a surface or into a cavity; endocrine glands are ductless, releasing hormones directly into the bloodstream. Mixed glands (e.g. pancreas, ovaries, testes) contain both exocrine and endocrine tissue.

blocks.x: Glandular secretion follows the classic secretory pathway: the protein product is made in the rough endoplasmic reticulum, packaged into secretory granules by the Golgi apparatus, and released from the cell by exocytosis.

blocks.name: Unicellular exocrine gland
blocks.def: A single glandular cell scattered within an epithelial sheet, e.g. the <term d="A single mucus-secreting cell scattered within an epithelium.">goblet cell</term> — found in the intestinal and respiratory epithelium, producing mucin (which combines with water to form protective, lubricating mucus).

blocks.name: Multicellular exocrine glands
blocks.def: Include mucus-secreting glands, sweat (sudoriferous) glands, oil (sebaceous) glands, salivary glands, the liver, and the pancreas. Made of two basic parts: a duct and a secretory unit.

blocks.name: Simple vs. compound glands
blocks.def: Classified by duct branching — simple glands have an unbranched duct; compound glands have a branching duct.

blocks.name: Tubular, alveolar & tubuloalveolar glands
blocks.def: Classified by the shape of the secretory unit — tubular (tube-shaped), alveolar/acinar (flask-shaped), or tubuloalveolar/tubuloacinar (a tube ending in a sac-like dilation).

blocks.name: Intercalated ducts
blocks.def: Small, lightly-stained, low cuboidal ducts within a gland lobule that help modify secretions.

blocks.name: Striated ducts
blocks.def: Columnar ducts with basal striations, also within a gland lobule, that further modify secretions by absorbing/adding specific components.

blocks.name: Interlobular (excretory) ducts
blocks.def: Larger ducts between lobules, lined by simple columnar, stratified columnar, or stratified cuboidal epithelium, that carry the final secretion out of the gland.

blocks.name: Serous glands
blocks.def: Have well-developed intercalated and striated ducts that actively modify the secretion. Produce a watery, protein-rich secretion; apical cytoplasm often stains intensely with eosin.

blocks.name: Mucous glands
blocks.def: Have poorly developed intercalated ducts (often unrecognizable) and no striated ducts, since the mucous secretion isn't modified further. Cytoplasm often appears "empty" in H&E stain since the mucus is water-soluble and washed out during processing.

blocks.name: Mixed (seromucous) glands
blocks.def: Contain both serous and mucous secretory units in variable proportions — e.g. the submandibular salivary gland.

blocks.name: Merocrine secretion
blocks.def: Product released by exocytosis, with no loss of cell material. Examples: salivary glands, pancreas, sweat glands.

blocks.name: Holocrine secretion
blocks.def: The entire cell disintegrates (a form of programmed cell death/apoptosis) to release its product. Examples: sebaceous glands, tarsal (Meibomian) glands of the eyelid.

blocks.name: Apocrine secretion
blocks.def: The apical portion of the cell pinches off along with the secretory product. Examples: mammary glands, apocrine sweat glands, ciliary (Moll's) glands of the eyelid, ceruminous (earwax) glands.

blocks.name: Endocrine gland (definition)
blocks.def: A ductless gland that releases hormones into the extracellular space; hormones then enter the blood and travel to specific target organs.

blocks.name: Classic endocrine glands
blocks.def: The pituitary, thyroid, parathyroid, adrenal, and pineal glands.

blocks.name: Other hormone-secreting tissue
blocks.def: Many organs are not exclusively classified as endocrine glands but contain hormone-secreting cells — including the hypothalamus, thymus, pancreas, ovaries, testes, kidneys, stomach, liver, small intestine, skin, heart, <term d="Fat tissue — connective tissue packed with cells that store energy and insulate.">adipose tissue</term>, and placenta.

blocks.name: Arrangement of endocrine secretory tissue
blocks.def: Endocrine secretory cells are typically arranged in cords, follicles, clumps, or plates.
